meta.title: OUniverse fact check
meta.statusNote: Status is judged as of 29 September 2026. Several missions changed state in 2026 (SMILE, Roman, Swift, PLATO, BepiColombo).

c.q: Yellow dwarf at the centre of the Solar System, holds it together by gravity, more than 99% of its mass.
OU researches solar physics, internal structure and space weather, models the solar wind and its interaction with planetary atmospheres.
c.note: No OU solar-physics group or project found. OU space-weather links found are SMILE (with the Met Office) and CEI detector work. Ask the School of Physical Sciences which work this refers to.

e.to: The Open University studies how the solar wind interacts with Earth's magnetic field through the ESA–CAS SMILE mission, whose X-ray camera detectors were developed and tested at the OU's Centre for Electronic Imaging.

sug.why: Replaces the unverified paragraph with documented OU work. Keep the original instead if the solar-physics work is confirmed.

c.q: Smallest planet, closest to the Sun, heavily cratered, geologically quiet, high density and a large metallic core.
“Possesses a surprisingly strong magnetic field.”
c.note: The field is weak, about 1% of Earth’s. What surprised scientists is that it exists at all. Suggest “a magnetic field, which is surprising for such a small planet”.

e.from: Despite its small size, it possesses a surprisingly strong magnetic field and a high density that suggests a massive metallic core.
e.to: Despite its small size, it has a global magnetic field, which is surprising for such a small planet, and a high density that suggests a massive metallic core.

c.q: OU scientists have studied Mercury’s surface composition and volcanic history for decades.
c.note: David Rothery (OU) has been UK lead scientist for MIXS since 2006, leads ESA’s Mercury Surface & Composition Working Group, and publishes on Mercury volcanism.

c.q: Research “helps explain how such a small planet could maintain a liquid outer core”.
c.note: No OU paper on Mercury’s core found. OU Mercury work is on surface composition and volcanism. Ask David Rothery.

e.from: This ongoing research helps explain how such a small planet could maintain a liquid outer core so close to the Sun.
e.to: An OU scientist is the UK lead for BepiColombo's MIXS X-ray spectrometer, which will map the elements on Mercury's surface.

c.q: “Successfully entered orbit around Mercury in late 2025.”
c.note: Not yet. Orbit insertion is scheduled for 21 November 2026, and the two orbiters separate on 9 and 10 December 2026. Science starts in spring 2027. Suggest “arrives at Mercury in November 2026”.

e.from: successfully entered orbit around Mercury in late 2025
e.to: is due to enter orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026

c.q: Joint ESA–JAXA mission with two orbiters (MPO and Mio) studying the surface, composition and magnetic field. Launched 2018.
OU academics are on the M-CAM monitoring camera team analysing flyby images.
c.note: ESA credits David Rothery (team member) and Jack Wright (M-CAM imaging team coordinator), both OU.

s.t: ESA: Top three images from the sixth Mercury flyby

c.q: OU was a development partner, with instrument lead the University of Leicester, on MIXS.
c.note: Leicester says MIXS was “jointly developed by the University of Leicester, the Open University, the University of Helsinki and partners”.

s.t: Bunce et al. 2020, Space Sci Rev

c.q: Live mission data is integrated into PhD projects and undergraduate teaching.
c.note: No public source. Ask the OU planetary science teaching team.

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm the teaching and PhD use with the OU planetary team.

c.q: Status “Operational”.
c.note: Correct for a working spacecraft, though it is still arriving. “En Route” would match JUICE and Hera until 21 November 2026.

c.q: Earth’s twin in size, thick CO₂ atmosphere and runaway greenhouse, retrograde rotation, surface hot enough to melt lead, sulfuric acid clouds.
“The OU leads international research into the Martian-like volcanic history of Venus”, plus atmospheric models of Venus’s evolution.
c.note: No source for OU leading Venus volcanism research, and “Martian-like” is unusual wording. The documented OU Venus work is EnVision’s VenSpec-U (Manish Patel’s group). Consider rewriting around that.

e.to: The Open University is helping to prepare ESA's EnVision mission to Venus. With a £2.3 million ESA grant, an OU team leads the testing and characterisation of the detectors in the VenSpec-U ultraviolet spectrometer, which will study the sulphur chemistry of Venus's clouds, and takes part in science preparations for the mission.

sug.why: Replaces unsourced claims with the documented EnVision role.

c.q: Only known planet with life, N₂–O₂ atmosphere, plate tectonics, liquid water in the habitable zone.
OU develops machine learning for satellite imagery to track deforestation, urban growth and glacial retreat, and supports international climate efforts.
c.note: No OU publication or project found. Ask the OU Earth observation researchers (School of Environment, Earth & Ecosystem Sciences).

sug.keep: Keep. Ask the OU Earth observation researchers for a project or paper to cite.

c.q: Modular microgravity laboratory. Partners are the US, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. First module launched 1998.
“The OU flew the BIOlogy and Mars Experiment (BIOMEX).”
c.note: BIOMEX was led by DLR (PI Jean-Pierre de Vera). The OU was a participant: Karen Olsson-Francis (OU) is a co-author of the mission paper. Suggest “OU scientists took part in BIOMEX”.

e.from: The OU flew the BIOlogy and Mars Experiment (BIOMEX) aboard
e.to: OU scientists took part in the DLR-led BIOlogy and Mars Experiment (BIOMEX) aboard

c.q: Mounted outside Zvezda on EXPOSE-R2. Bacteria, algae, lichens and fungi exposed to vacuum, UV and temperature extremes.
“For 533 days.”
c.note: Published figures are 531 days in space for the biological samples (vacuum exposure about 532 days). The exposure period itself ran from 22 October 2014 to 3 February 2016 (469 days). Pick one figure and match it to a source.

e.from: for 533 days
e.to: for about 18 months

c.q: Samples returned with Tim Peake in June 2016.
c.note: 18 June 2016, Soyuz TMA-19M.

s.t: ESA: Expose-R2 samples back on Earth

c.q: Launched 1990, three decades of observations, contributed to the age of the universe and the discovery of dark energy.
WFC3’s CCDs are built by Teledyne e2v, which partners closely with the OU’s Centre for Electronic Imaging.
c.note: WFC3 UVIS uses two e2v CCD43 detectors. The CEI is a joint OU–Teledyne e2v centre.

c.q: OU astronomers use the Hubble archive to study stellar populations and galaxy evolution, and it feeds the astronomy curriculum.
c.note: Plausible but no specific project found. Ask the OU astronomy group.

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm with the OU astronomy group.

c.q: “A constellation of two satellites.”
c.note: Three now: Sentinel-2C launched 5 September 2024, and 2A continues in an extended campaign alongside 2B and 2C.

e.from: Sentinel-2 is a constellation of two satellites
e.to: Sentinel-2 is a constellation of satellites, currently three,

c.q: High-resolution optical imaging for Copernicus: vegetation, soil, water, frequent revisits.
OU machine learning for soil moisture, forest fire evolution and desertification risk, and student training.
c.note: No OU-authored Sentinel-2 study found. Ask the OU team for the paper or project.

sug.keep: Keep. Ask for the OU paper or project to cite.

c.q: Ocean and land monitoring: sea-surface topography, temperature and colour.
OU combines Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-2 data for high-resolution evapotranspiration in forests.
c.note: This technique exists (for example ESA’s SEN-ET project and Guzinski & Nieto 2019), but those papers are by DHI and others, not the OU. Ask for the OU publication.

sug.keep: Keep. Ask for the OU paper or project to cite.

c.q: Proposed Canadian-led UV and blue-optical space telescope with a field far wider than Hubble’s, for cosmology and galaxy formation.
CEI awarded £2.1 million for testing and space qualification of UV detectors for CASTOR, a Canadian-led 1 m telescope targeting about 2030.
CIS303 and CIS120 detectors from Teledyne e2v. Electro-optical testing, space qualification, and comparison of UV coatings and enhancement.

s.t: OU CEI SPIE paper: path to CASTOR

c.q: OU helps define the telescope’s survey strategy.
c.note: Not found. The UK CASTOR consortium is led by UKATC. Ask Jesper Skottfelt (CEI).

e.from: spaceflight, alongside OU involvement in helping define the telescope's survey strategy.
e.to: spaceflight.

c.q: UK-led, delivered by ESA, a “gold standard” climate calibration mission measuring incoming and reflected radiation.
CEI radiation-damage study of the Teledyne e2v CIS120: dark current, noise and QE before and after gamma and proton irradiation at several temperatures.
The CIS120 is “being evaluated for TRUTHS”.
c.note: The CIS120 study found does not name TRUTHS. Ask the CEI whether TRUTHS is a named customer for this work.

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm with the CEI that TRUTHS is a named target for the CIS120 work.

c.q: “Launched in April 2026.”
c.note: Launched 19 May 2026 on Vega-C. The 9 April date was postponed.

s.t: ESA: Smile set to launch on 19 May

e.from: launched in April 2026
e.to: launched on 19 May 2026

c.q: ESA–CAS mission for the first global X-ray images of the magnetosphere and its interaction with the solar wind.
Twin CCD370s, 4510 × 4510 pixels of 18 µm, form the SXI focal plane. The CEI tested noise, CTI and defects before flight.

s.t: Parsons et al. 2023: SXI flight CCD370 characterisation

c.q: “Adapted from the CCD270s flown on PLATO.”
c.note: PLATO has not flown (launch now March 2027). The CCD370 derives from the CCD270 developed for PLATO. Suggest “developed for PLATO”.

e.from: adapted from the CCD270s flown on PLATO
e.to: derived from the CCD270s developed for PLATO

c.q: “The Centre for Electronic Imaging designed … the detectors.”
c.note: The OU says the CEI has spent over a decade “developing and testing” them. Teledyne e2v manufactures them. “Developed and characterised” is safer than “designed”.

e.from: designed and characterised the twin CCD370 detectors
e.to: developed and tested the twin CCD370 detectors

c.q: “The university is now analysing the mission’s early X-ray images.”
c.note: The OU launch article covers optimising CCD performance and work with the Met Office. No source on early images. Check with the CEI before keeping this.

e.from: The university is now analysing the mission's early X-ray images of how the solar wind interacts with Earth's magnetosphere.
e.to: The team is now using modelling and experiments to get the best performance from the detectors in flight.

c.q: Status “Decommissioned”.
c.note: Swift has not been decommissioned. A commercial reboost failed in August 2026, and it resumed UVOT and XRT science. NASA expects re-entry around the end of 2026. Use “Operational” for now, then “Re-entered”.

e.from: Decommissioned
e.to: Operational

sug.why: Change again to a re-entered status when Swift re-enters, expected around the end of 2026.

c.q: Gamma-ray burst observatory that slews to afterglows, operating for over 20 years.
OU astronomers use Swift data to teach transient astrophysics.
c.note: No public source. Ask the OU astronomy teaching team.

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm with the OU astronomy teaching team.

c.q: First UK Space Agency mission, a CubeSat technology demonstrator. Completed after about 14 months of operations.
Payloads for space weather and secure communications.
c.note: TOPCAT measured the ionosphere with GPS. JANUS tested random-number generation for secure communications. FUNcube provided education.

c.q: CEI won one of three science payload slots for C3D. Launched July 2014, three cameras, first in-orbit test of a European 0.18 µm CMOS imager. Dark-current and flatband shifts like CCDs, plus single-event upsets.
The data “has since informed the design of more radiation-tolerant space CMOS sensors”.
c.note: Plausible (C3D2 followed on AlSat Nano) but not stated in a source. Ask the CEI.

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm with the CEI.

c.q: Only natural satellite, drives tides, stabilises Earth’s axis, regolith and mare basalts, only other body humans have visited.
“The OU leads international efforts in lunar research, focusing on the extraction of water and oxygen from regolith … mass spectrometers … permanently shadowed craters.”
c.note: The OU does lead ProSPA (ESA PROSPECT) and built the PITMS and EMS-L mass spectrometers, so the instrument part is right. “Leads international efforts in lunar research” is too broad for a source to support. Suggest naming ProSPA.

e.from: The OU leads international efforts in lunar research, focusing on the extraction of water and oxygen from the moon's regolith.
e.to: The OU leads the development of instruments that search for water and oxygen in the Moon's regolith, including ProSPA, the analytical laboratory of ESA's PROSPECT package.

c.q: Work is essential for Artemis missions.
c.note: No documented OU Artemis role found. PROSPECT flies on a NASA CLPS lander, which is part of the wider Artemis programme.

e.from: This work is essential for the success of future sustainable lunar bases and the upcoming Artemis missions.
e.to: This work supports plans for sustainable future exploration of the Moon.

c.q: India’s first lunar probe. International instruments, 3D mapping and mineralogy, evidence of water molecules, operated about ten months.
c.note: Launched 22 October 2008, contact lost 29 August 2009, so about ten months. The file’s “nearly a year” is fine.

c.q: CEI proton radiation assessment of C1XS’s 24 CCD54 detectors using SPENVIS. 14 modules characterised and ten recommended. Continuing advisory role.
landed_coords lat 42, lon −58.5.
c.note: Actual site (Statio Tianchuan) is 43.06° N, 51.92° W, so lon should be about −51.9. The current value is about 200 km off.

c.q: Returned about 2 kg (1,731 g) in December 2020 from young mare basalts in Oceanus Procellarum. Automated docking in lunar orbit.
“One of only seven international scientists selected … loan beginning in April 2025.”
c.note: CNSA named seven institutions from six countries on 24 April 2025, and the OU was one. Mahesh Anand then collected 60 mg in China. “Loan beginning in April 2025” should read “awarded in April 2025”.

s.t: Science: foreign scientists awarded lunar samples

e.from: An Open University academic was one of only seven international scientists selected to receive samples from the Chang'e-5 mission, with the loan beginning in April 2025.
e.to: In April 2025 the Open University was one of only seven institutions outside China selected to borrow samples from the Chang'e-5 mission.

c.q: Measuring C, N, O and noble-gas isotopes to test the giant-impact theory.
c.note: Oxygen isotopes are confirmed in the Science article. Carbon, nitrogen and noble gases are not stated publicly. Ask Mahesh Anand.

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm the carbon, nitrogen and noble-gas work with Mahesh Anand.

c.q: ProSPA is attached to Luna 27.
c.note: After 2022 ESA ended its Luna cooperation with Russia. PROSPECT (including the OU-led ProSPA) now flies on NASA CLPS CP-22, the Intuitive Machines IM-4 Nova-C lander, launching 2027 to about 84.5° S, 31.5° E. Consider renaming or replacing this entry (see the Missing missions tab).

e.from: Luna 27 entry
e.to: Replace with a PROSPECT entry for the Intuitive Machines IM-4 lander (see Missing missions): status Planned, launch_year 2027, landed_coords {lat:-84.5, lon:31.5}. Keep the ProSPA paragraph.

sug.why: Structural change. Claude will ask before renaming, because the name is used as a key.

c.q: The OU leads development of ProSPA, which heats drilled samples and analyses them by mass spectrometry.
Supported by RAL Space, Airbus, the Max Planck Institute and TU Munich.
c.note: ESA’s page mentions subcontractors in eight countries without naming them. TU Munich appears in the science team (Ulrich Walter). Ask the ProSPA team (Simeon Barber).

sug.keep: Keep. Confirm the partner list with the ProSPA team.

c.q: Luna 27 is a Russian robotic south-polar lander with a drill for volatiles.
“Search for liquid water and ice at the lunar south pole.”

e.to: search for water ice and other volatiles

c.q: Heritage from flight hardware on Rosetta (Ptolemy) and Beagle 2 (GAP).
